title: Linear LOCAL versus constant dynamic locality for a promise-free LCL
formal: Does there exist one promise-free LCL on bounded-degree graphs that has a deterministic incremental dynamic-LOCAL algorithm with O(1) repair radius, but requires Ω(n) rounds in deterministic LOCAL? Under the models below, the answer is no: combining the cited simulations gives a deterministic O(√n·polylog n)-round LOCAL algorithm whenever constant dynamic locality is possible.
definitions: A promise-free LCL Π has one fixed degree bound Δ≥2, one fixed checking radius r≥1, finite vertex input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r input/output neighborhoods. A labeling is legal exactly when all vertices pass this check. The problem must admit a legal output for every finite simple undirected graph of degree at most Δ and every input assignment, including disconnected graphs. Legality is invariant under isomorphism and does not depend on identifiers, port orders, or graph size. No assumption of bipartiteness, planarity, a rooted structure, or a special global input encoding is made. In deterministic LOCAL, vertices initially know n, their own input, degree, ports, and a distinct identifier in [n²]. They exchange unbounded messages with neighbors in synchronous rounds. One finite computable program must work on every input, with unrestricted terminating local computation. Round complexity is the worst case over input graphs, labels, ports, and identifiers. In incremental dynamic-LOCAL, a central deterministic algorithm starts with the empty graph and a known upper bound N on the eventual number of vertices. An adversary inserts isolated vertices with immutable input labels and identifiers, or inserts edges between existing vertices, always respecting Δ and the size bound. After every event the algorithm must maintain a legal output on the entire current graph. Existing outputs may change only within distance R(N) of an endpoint of the inserted edge, or of the inserted vertex, measured after the event. The algorithm may inspect the entire revealed graph and retain arbitrary state, but future vertices, inputs, and edges are unknown. The locality is the largest radius of any output change, not the number of changes or the update time. All algorithms are uniform finite programs, all local computation must terminate, and all guarantees are deterministic and worst case. A constant locality bound is independent of size and may depend only on the fixed problem. A linear lower bound means that for every correct algorithm A there are a constant c_A>0 and arbitrarily large size bounds with an input or update sequence forcing locality at least c_A times that bound. This infinitely-often formulation is already ruled out by a uniform sublinear upper bound.
answer_criterion: A positive answer would require one finite total LCL specification, a constant-radius dynamic algorithm, and a linear deterministic LOCAL lower bound. A negative answer rules out this combination for every such LCL. The latter follows from the sublinear simulation described below; this is a derived corollary, not a claim that either cited paper states this exact saved question verbatim.
context:
Dynamic computation retains the history of how a graph was built. This history can provide choices that a fresh synchronous computation has to establish through communication. The saved question asks whether local repairs could exploit that advantage so strongly that a constant repair radius replaces a linear number of communication rounds.

The requirement to work on every bounded-degree graph and every input matters. Special graph families may have global promises that affect what an algorithm can infer from a partial view. Here all intermediate graphs are valid inputs to the same total problem, so the simulations can build disjoint copies, delete edges, and introduce isolated vertices without leaving the problem’s domain.

A constant-radius dynamic algorithm yields a constant-locality online algorithm. On each online request, reveal a slightly larger constant-radius neighborhood and simulate its vertex and edge insertions. Once a requested vertex is labeled, later revelations are too far away to change it. This uses the incremental model beginning with an empty graph; unseen input labels are not supplied in advance.

The first step removes dependence on unrelated revealed components. Lemma 7.5 turns an online algorithm of locality T(n) into one whose decision depends only on its current revealed component, with locality T(2^O(n³)). If T is a constant, this enormous change of the size argument leaves locality constant. The family of all bounded-degree graphs satisfies the lemma’s closure assumptions.

The second step simulates that component-wise algorithm in sublinear deterministic LOCAL time. The clustering framework separates small-diameter regions with only O(√n) leftover vertices. Grouping nearby leftovers gives components of diameter O(√n) whose constant-radius views are mutually separate. Each such component can simulate the deterministic online rule on its leftovers independently; these simulations form one valid online prefix. Each remaining region can then choose a compatible completion by finite exhaustive search. Local checkability makes the separate completions compatible. The total communication radius is O(√n·polylog n). This explains the deterministic specialization of the component-wise simulation.

Combining these steps gives dynamic O(1) → online O(1) → deterministic LOCAL O(√n·polylog n). Since √n times any fixed polylogarithm is o(n), a linear LOCAL lower bound is impossible. Smaller separations can still exist; the result only rules out the specified linear-versus-constant target.
why: The question probes the limits of using construction history to replace communication for locally verifiable tasks. Its negative resolution places a general upper bound on that advantage and demonstrates why exact size regimes and the absence of promises matter when comparing locality models.

importance.reason: A broad model-separation benchmark resolved through general simulation machinery. Retained for its structural meaning and traceability, with resolved status rather than counted as a remaining open problem.

progress.text: The locality framework establishes the simulations from LOCAL to incremental dynamic-LOCAL to online-LOCAL, and studies their differences for locally checkable tasks.

The updated problem list asks for a promise-free linear LOCAL versus constant dynamic separation. The corrected comparison paper provides the component-wise conversion needed for the later implication.

The revised quantum-advantage paper extends the clustering simulation to component-wise online locality on general graphs. Its deterministic constant-locality specialization has O(√n·polylog n) LOCAL complexity.

Composing dynamic-to-online simulation, the constant-locality component-wise conversion, and the sublinear LOCAL simulation rules out the requested witness. The card records the derivation explicitly; no withdrawn dynamic derandomization theorem is invoked.

status_note: Resolved negatively in the fixed standard deterministic incremental model as a corollary of the cited model simulations and the August 2026 component-wise simulation. The chain of implications is spelled out in context. The original open statement is retained for history; the result does not classify all smaller dynamic/LOCAL separations.
